newsitem.title: USA: Alyeska whistleblower program gets mixed reviews.
newsitem.headline: Alyeska whistleblower program gets mixed reviews.

text.p: Many workers still fear harassment and retaliation if they report environmental and safety problems along the trans-Alaska oil pipeline, said a study released on Tuesday by the U.S. Bureau of Land Management.

The study, compiled from 1,356 survey responses and followup interviews with workers, whistleblowers and overseers, gave mixed reviews of the employee concerns program set up in late 1995 by Alyeska Pipeline Service Co., operator of the 800-mile (1,300-km) line and its Valdez marine terminal.
The program was established after a rash of worker complaints and congressional inquiries into trans-Alaska pipeline system shortcomings.
The BLM report contained 23 findings and recommendations for changes to make the whistleblower-protection program more effective.

"Alyeska has made much progress in the past few years, but more remains to be done in providing a work atmosphere free from fear of retaliation for expressing concerns," Assistant Secretary of Interior Bob Armstrong said in a statement released by the BLM.
"This report shows that the 'shoot the messenger' attitude, although more subtle than before, continues in some quarters at Alyeska, particularly in the contract work force," Armstrong said.

A slight majority of workers, and a large majority of supervisors, said Alyeska's corporate culture has improved in recent years, the report said. Others said they have little faith that they will be protected if they point out flaws.
While 41 percent of Alyeska employees said the company's corporate culture has failed to improve, 51 percent of contract employees held that opinion, according the report.
"The contractors, as opposed to Alyeska, have not had the white-hot light of publicity focused on them in the past, as Alyeska has," said Rob McWhorter, a BLM spokesman.
Contract employees make up about half of the pipeline system workforce.
Whistleblower complaints continue, and "there is evidence that harassment still exists," McWhorter said.

The Joint Pipeline Office, the consortium of federal and state agencies -- including the BLM -- that oversee Alyeska operations, ordered Alyeska to come up with a plan by April 18 to correct problems identified in the report, McWhorter said.
To Alyeska, the study showed that the company made some progress in its reform efforts, said company spokeswoman Jennifer Ruys.
"We think it was a thorough and fair report," she said.
Alyeska has already started action on some of the recommendations, including having the manager of the employee concerns program report directly to the company's president, Ruys said.
A corporate reorganization will also put more officials in the field to hear complaints of whistle-blowers and protect them from retailiation, she said.
Other steps are planned to get the proper message to Alyeska contractors, "to make it clear that they will be in this new culture that we want to instill in this organization," she said.

Alyeska is owned by seven oil companies with interests on Alaska's North Slope. Major owners are British Petroleum, Atlantic Richfield and Exxon. Mobil, Unocal Phillips Petroleum and Amerada Hess own minor shares.
